name: Tiktokmaxxing

lead: Tiktokmaxxing is a looksmaxxing term for optimising your look and content for TikTok-driven attraction. Forum users describe a target aesthetic: a longer fluffy fringe or curtains haircut, clear skin, defined bone structure, bold brows and a trendy wardrobe.[1][2]

Proponents on looksmax.org say that this style, rather than the classic tall "maesthetic" look, is what younger audiences respond to, and that people with limited facial potential can still ascend by adopting it.[2][3] These are community claims; no published study tests them.

paras: Posts recommend a longer hairstyle with short sides, clear skin, trimmed or filled-in brows, coloured contacts, gym training and sometimes procedures such as jaw filler.[2] Another thread says a video's early views come from the algorithm but continued momentum depends on likes, which it attributes to looking attractive.[1]

Some forum suggestions involve medical or surgical products and procedures, which carry their own risks and are covered in their own entries. The trend is also tied to a particular moment and audience, as proponents themselves note by dating it to 2022.[3]

angle.text: Tiktokmaxxing is a styling package: haircut, skin, brows, clothes and contacts. Users adopt it hoping to look like the aesthetic they see succeeding on the platform.

lead: Tiktokmaxxing is looksmaxxing slang for tailoring appearance and content toward what performs on TikTok and what younger audiences are reported to find attractive. A 2022 looksmax.org thread describes the target as a "prettyboy" aesthetic with fluffy curtains or fringe, full lips, bold brows, thick lashes, a tan and baggy designer clothes.[1] Most of the items on that list are styling choices, which is why the idea is framed in the community as one of the more accessible routes to a better-looking presentation.

Posters present it as an alternative route for people with limited facial "PSL" potential. One thread claims many TikTok prettyboys are around 5 PSL in face and succeed through styling: a longer haircut, clear skin, a defined jaw, brow grooming and contacts.[2] PSL is the community's numerical scale for rating facial attractiveness, which grew out of forums such as PUAHate, Sluthate and Lookism.[3]

Another post argues the platform algorithm gives a video initial reach, but that sustained virality depends on likes, which the poster links to attractiveness.[4] These accounts are anecdotal, and no published research has examined whether a particular TikTok aesthetic increases attention or attraction. The broader looksmaxxing phenomenon, which TikTok creators helped bring to a mass audience in the early 2020s, has drawn extensive news and academic commentary [3][5][6].
infobox: Fringe or curtains hair, clear skin, brows, contacts, trendy clothes[2][1]

paras: The term refers to optimising look and content for TikTok-driven attraction. Proponents describe a consistent set of features: a longer haircut, smooth skin, defined jaw, brow grooming and colourful contacts.[2][1]

In the community's vocabulary the look is contrasted with the "maesthetic" ideal of a tall, angular, classically masculine man. The 2022 thread that popularised the slogan "TikTokmaxx or death" argues that the two are in competition for the attention of women under 25.[1]

Tiktokmaxxing sits within what the wider scene calls softmaxxing, the non-invasive end of looksmaxxing covering skincare, grooming, clothing and fitness, as opposed to hardmaxxing, which covers surgery, off-label drugs and other extreme measures.[3] A researcher writing in The Conversation in January 2024 likewise describes grooming, teeth whitening, hair removal and mewing as the entry level of the trend.[6]

Looksmaxxing itself emerged on incel-linked forums in the 2010s and reached TikTok in the early 2020s, where male creators popularised the word, often framing it at first as self-improvement and sometimes with humour.[3] Tiktokmaxxing as a distinct term appears on looksmax.org in threads from 2022, dated by the posters themselves to that year's perceived TikTok style.[4][2][1]

The hairstyle at the centre of the look had a separate life on the platform. Refinery29 described the curtain fringe as the TikTok haircut trend of winter 2020, noting that #curtainbangs had passed five million video views and crediting ordinary users rather than a single originator.[7] In April 2025 the trend site Ypulse reported that the floppy, centre-parted 1990s style, nicknamed "curtains" for men, was spreading from TikTok to red carpets, and tied it partly to nostalgia and to pop-culture figures who blur traditional masculine norms.[8]

Forum members tend to treat these style shifts as evidence that the prevailing "pheno" changes with the audience and the year. One poster says his "maesthetic" friend, whom he rates almost PSL 6, was approached mainly by older women while TikTok-styled men did better on dating apps; the thread's title says the style was required "in 2022".[1]

As described in forum posts, the package begins with hair: a longer cut such as a fringe, curtains or a fluffy, curly top with shorter sides, with advice to address thinning or poor hair quality by whatever means a user prefers.[2] Skin comes next, with posters urging a clear, smooth complexion and either a shave or stubble.[2]

Other elements named include reducing facial bloat for a more defined bone structure, coloured contact lenses, trimming heavy brows or using brow and lash growth products on sparse ones, and gym training.[2] The same thread lists jaw filler and a canthoplasty or canthopexy for a tighter, upward-tilted eye shape, and mentions SARMs among gym aids; these are medical or surgical items that carry their own risks and are covered under their own entries.[2]

A second thread, written by a poster who says he is not a TikTok user but has a brother and a gym friend with accounts of 57,000 and 700,000 followers, describes a video's first reach as coming from the algorithm and its further growth as depending on likes.[4] The poster reports that his brother's car videos stalled around 1,000 views while a switch to gym videos brought around 30,000 views on the first upload.[4]

Community replies are mixed in tone. Some commenters in these threads joke about deepfaking a user into popular TikTok videos, one says an accidental middle part drew unprompted compliments, and others reply that height or a recessed face limit what styling can do.[4][2]

A 2022 post claims women under 25 prefer a TikTok-style prettyboy over a taller, classically masculine "maesthetic" man, citing a friend's dating results and a conversation with a woman on Discord.[1]

Another post suggests the style is accessible to anyone with limited facial potential and lists steps from hair and skin to jaw fillers and canthoplasty.[2] A further thread claims algorithmic reach starts videos but likes sustain them.[4]
A reply in the 2022 thread offers a different reading: that younger women may simply favour more youthful features, while adding that it is unclear what "ideal" now means.[1]
No published studies have examined whether a particular TikTok aesthetic increases attention or attraction. The claims above are forum opinion and personal anecdote.

Commentary on the surrounding looksmaxxing scene comes from several academics. Rachel Rodgers, an applied psychology professor at Northeastern University, told that university's news service that looksmaxxing is a growing industry across appearance, entertainment and health markets, that dating apps have made dating "increasingly hypervisual", and that companies are now marketing to men, who were "the last frontier".[5] Her colleague Nathan Blake links the trend to the "quantified self" and the attention economy, and says some men's sense of lacking control may feed the pursuit.[5]

Jamilla Rosdahl, a senior lecturer at the Australian College of Applied Psychology, wrote in The Conversation that looksmaxxing may look like self-care but is connected to incel culture, and argued that platform recommendation algorithms can lead young men toward harmful content.[6] Wikipedia's article on looksmaxxing summarises similar concerns about body dysmorphia and notes that some men report benefits such as dating success and peer approval.[3]
No studies found.

The soft items in the package, such as a haircut, skincare and clothing, carry the ordinary risks of those products. The procedural items that appear in some threads, including filler, eyelid or canthal surgery and performance drugs, are medical interventions with their own adverse-event profiles.[2]

Experts quoted in news coverage of looksmaxxing generally raise psychological rather than physical concerns for the styling end of the scene: appearance comparison, body-image strain and social isolation.[5][6]

On looksmax.org the idea is discussed both as a styling route for users who feel limited by bone structure and as a hypothesis about what younger audiences find attractive in a given year.[2][1] Because the community treats the target look as year-specific, the term is often used with a date attached.[1]
